title: Reservations in two countries
summary: MesaLista books tables at 2,000 restaurants in Mexico and Texas. Payments need transactions and favorites are written in both countries.

requirements.1: {{s1}} keeps payments in managed MySQL without leaving Mexico, with a copy in another zone that takes over on its own if the primary fails.
requirements.2: {{s2}} gives reporting a separate copy of the slot 1 primary so it does not slow it down, even if the copy runs a few seconds behind.
requirements.3: {{s3}} stores favorites: each country writes in milliseconds to its own region and both accept writes. The other region sees them later, because availability is preferred over consistency.
requirements.4: {{s4}} alerts the reporting team if the slot 2 copy falls more than 30 seconds behind the primary.
requirements.5: {{s5}} keeps the database password out of the code: the app requests it at startup and, before the password expires, the service sends a notice so your own function changes it.
requirements.6: The pilot restaurant's MySQL runs on its own premises; its payments are migrated to slot 1 before opening to all 2,000 restaurants.

s1.explanation: With zone-redundant HA, Flexible Server keeps a standby in another zone of the same region; if the primary becomes unavailable, the standby becomes the primary. The standby serves no reads or writes.

s2.explanation: The Flexible Server read replica uses asynchronous replication, with a measurable delay, and serves as the source for reporting; that way the primary only handles the writes.

s3.explanation: With multi-region writes, Cosmos DB commits each write in the local region and replicates it to the others asynchronously; that is why this setup does not support strong consistency.

s4.explanation: Flexible Server publishes the Replication Lag In Seconds metric and the replica guide recommends an alert for when the lag crosses a threshold; an Azure Monitor metric alert sends that notice.

s5.explanation: Key Vault stores the password as a secret the app reads. Thirty days before it expires, Key Vault publishes the near expiry event to Event Grid and your own function changes it; the validity period goes in the ValidityPeriodDays tag.

azure-mysql-flex-ha.s2: The HA standby is not available for reads or writes: it is passive and only exists for a fast failover.

azure-mysql-read-replica.s1: There is no automatic failover between the source and the read replica: to use it you stop replication manually.

azure-sql-database.s1: Active geo-replication belongs to Azure SQL Database, not MySQL, and its geo-secondary only serves read-only queries.
azure-sql-database.s2: Active geo-replication copies an Azure SQL Database; it is not a copy of the slot 1 MySQL.
azure-sql-database.s3: In active geo-replication transactions are committed on the primary and the geo-secondary only serves reads: there are not two regions writing.

azure-activity-log.s4: The activity log records management operations, such as creating or changing a resource; the replica lag is the Replication Lag In Seconds metric, and the alert on it is a metric alert.

azure-app-configuration.s5: App Configuration stores app settings and complements Key Vault, which is where secrets are stored; the near expiry notice through Event Grid in the rotation tutorial is published by Key Vault.
